food.text: In the 19th-century Ottoman palace, mutton, clarified butter, flour and rice were the most common ingredients. Butter and yogurt, made with milk from Egyptian and Dutch cows, were bought at the Üsküdar and Eyüp markets.

Beginning in the 19th century, the Ottomans began using French culinary terms at diplomatic events. French cuisine was then considered the epitome of culinary accomplishment, and its influence was felt in the Ottoman court and in other European courts.

Mehmet Kamil's influential 1844 manuscript includes recipes for tomato stew, stuffed tomato dolma and tomato pilaf. Tomatoes had entered Ottoman cuisine by the 1690s, but they are missing from the few recipe manuscripts that survive from the 18th century.

Beginning in the 19th century, the Ottomans began using French culinary terms at diplomatic events. Banquet menus for international dignitaries were written in French, and service à la russe replaced service à la française at formal dinners. Ottoman pilaf, börek and kebabs continued to be served.

Ayşe Fahriye's book Ev Kadını has recipes for both green tomatoes (kavata) and red tomatoes (domates). Some of them, such as tomato pilaf and dolma, are still common in modern Turkish cuisine. Her 1882 cookbook is the last mention of green tomatoes in Ottoman cooking.

Mutton, clarified butter, flour and rice were the most common ingredients in 19th-century Ottoman palace cuisine. Butter and yogurt were bought at the Üsküdar and Eyüp markets. The most common cheeses were kaşar, kaşkaval, tulum peyniri and beyaz peynir.

In the 19th century, food remained a symbol of Ottoman power and prestige. Adapting French culinary practices to palace cuisine reflected the Ottoman desire to prove themselves the cultural equal of Europeans.

Hunting for food was common in the Ottoman world. The 19th-century Ihlamur Pavilion in Istanbul was a hunting lodge designed by the Ottoman-Armenian architect Nikoğos Balyan for Sultan Abdulmejid I. Deer, wolves and foxes were all hunted, but rabbits were by far the most common game.

Ayşe Fahriye's cookbook Ev Kadını, from 1882, has recipes for both green tomatoes, called kavata, and red tomatoes, called domates. It is the last mention of green tomatoes in Ottoman cooking. Some of her recipes, such as tomato pilaf and dolma, are still common in modern Turkish cuisine.
A Syrian baklava recipe was introduced to the Turkish city of Gaziantep in 1871 by Çelebi Güllü, who had learned it from a chef in Damascus. It developed into the Gaziantep baklava known today.

art.text: During the 19th century, Ottoman architecture took in more and more influence from Western Europe. Ottoman Baroque continued into the early century, and Empire style and Neoclassical motifs were introduced. Eclecticism then became prominent, especially in the Tanzimat period that began in 1839.

Clock towers rose to prominence as a new type of monument in the Ottoman Empire over the 19th century. The largest and most impressive in Istanbul is the Dolmabahçe Clock Tower, built by Abdülhamid II in 1890 to 1894. It mixes late Baroque decoration with Neoclassical and eclectic style.

Istanbul became a new center of Art Nouveau after the Italian architect Raimondo D'Aronco arrived in the late 19th century. He came at the invitation of Sultan Abdülhamid II and served as chief court architect between 1896 and 1909. The style was most common in new apartment buildings, and a local flavour developed.

European-style painting was slow to be adopted in the Ottoman world, and Osman Hamdi Bey (1842 to 1910) was for long a somewhat solitary figure. He trained in Paris and painted throughout a long career as a senior administrator and curator. Many of his works show the subjects of Orientalism from the inside.

The 19th century brought growing Western European influence to Ottoman architecture. Styles shifted from Ottoman Baroque to Empire and Neoclassical motifs, then to eclecticism during the Tanzimat period. Dolmabaçe Palace and many mosques by architects of the Balyan family are examples.

In 1843 a weaving workshop was established at Hereke to supply the royal palaces with silk brocades and other textiles. In 1850 the cotton looms of the Hereke Imperial Factory were moved to a factory in Bakirkoy, west of Istanbul, and replaced by Jacquard looms.

A new painting technique, trompe-l'œil, was imported into the Ottoman Empire, and its effective use began under Abdülmecid I, who reigned from 1839 to 1861. In the Ortaköy Mosque, built in the 1850s, the painted dome shows neo-Renaissance architecture mixed with rows of Islamic-style mihrabs that replicate the mosque's actual mihrab below.

Painted decoration in the 19th century drew on a new European-influenced repertoire of garlands, ribbons, flower bouquets and baskets of roses. Murals of naturalistic landscapes also became common from the late 18th century onward, especially inside palaces.

The Nusretiye Mosque, built by Mahmud II between 1822 and 1826 at Tophane, was among the last fully Baroque monuments in the Ottoman Empire. Its name commemorates the "victory" Mahmud II won by destroying the Janissaries in 1826, the year the mosque was completed. During his reign, which lasted from 1808 to 1839, new European-influenced styles were introduced and replaced the Baroque.

Starting at the turn of the 19th century, Western classical music found much greater patronage at the Ottoman court, chiefly after the death of Mahmud II. Composers such as Donizetti Pasha were held in high esteem, while Ottoman music suffered official neglect. This led prominent composers, including Ismail Dede Efendi, to leave the court.
The Sirkeci Railway Station, terminus of the Orient Express, was designed in an Orientalist style by the German architect August Jasmund. It was built between 1888 and 1890.

Clock towers rose to prominence in Ottoman architecture over the 19th century, one of several new types of monument introduced in the era. They stood alongside railway stations as signs of the empire's modernisation.

The Dolmabahçe Palace, built between 1843 and 1856, also features trompe-l'œil painting. It mixes European and neo-Islamic motifs. A later example is the Pertevniyal Valide Sultan Mosque of 1871, whose decorative scheme blends European, Ottoman and Islamic revivalist motifs.

The Tomb of Nakşidil Sultan, mother of Mahmud II, was built in 1818 near the Fatih Mosque complex in Istanbul. It is one of the finest Ottoman Baroque tombs and also shows some Empire style influence. It was designed by the Ottoman Armenian architect Krikor Balian.

The Selimiye Barracks, the largest barracks of its time, was built in southern Üsküdar between 1800 and 1803. Revolting Janissaries burned it down in 1812. Mahmud II rebuilt it in stone between 1825 and 1828, and Abdulmecid expanded it to its current form between 1842 and 1853.

The largest and most impressive clock tower in Istanbul is the Dolmabahçe Clock Tower, built by Abdülhamid II in 1890–1894. It mixes late Baroque decoration with the Neoclassical and eclectic style of the 19th century.
A fire in 1878 caused extensive damage at the Hereke Imperial Factory and closed production until 1882. Carpet production began there in 1891, and Hereke became a center for expert carpet weavers.

The Çırağan Palace was completed in 1872 with a severe Neoclassical appearance and Orientalist decoration. Fire destroyed it in 1910, leaving only the seaside façade standing. That façade was later integrated into a hotel in 1987.

The Ayazma Mosque had its 18th-century decoration repainted in the 19th century. The same flower-vase motifs were kept, but they were rendered in shades of grey and black, a technique called grisaille.

war.text: Despite military reforms that reconstituted the Ottoman Modern Army, the Ottoman Empire lost its North African territories and the Dodecanese in the Italo-Turkish War (1911). It then lost almost all of its European territories in the Balkan Wars (1912–1913). After the First Balkan War, around 400,000 Muslims fled with the retreating Ottoman armies, many dying from cholera brought by the soldiers, and 400,000 non-Muslims fled territory still under Ottoman rule.

The Greek War of Independence started in 1821, and the Great Powers, including Russia, intervened from 1827 in support of the revolutionaries. The Treaty of Adrianople ended the war in 1829. It forced the Ottomans to accept Greek independence as the new Kingdom of Greece.

When Ottoman Turkey joined the war on the side of the Central Powers in 1914, it declared a jihad against the Entente States. The modern Ottoman army carried regimental flags with the state coat of arms on one side and the Shahada on the other, in gold writing on red.

In 1897 Greece attacked the Ottoman Empire to help the Second Cretan Uprising, but was defeated in Thessaly. Crete gained autonomy in 1898 after the Cretan Revolt. Thessaly had been ceded to Greece in 1881.
Ankara, a city in central Anatolia, was sacked in 1832 by Egyptians under Ibrahim Pasha. In the 19th century its population was estimated at between 20,000 and 60,000 people.

literature.text: Until the 19th century, Ottoman prose contained no fiction. There were no counterparts to the European romance, short story or novel, though similar genres existed to some extent in the Turkish folk tradition and in Divan poetry. Poetry, especially Divan poetry, was by far the dominant stream.

Many writers of the Tanzimat period wrote in several genres at once. This diversity was partly due to their wish to spread as much of the new literature as possible, in the hope that it would contribute to a revitalization of Ottoman social structure.

Poetry and song of the aşık tradition were almost exclusively oral until the 19th century, so much of it remains anonymous. Dadaloğlu (1785–1868) was one of the last great aşıks before the tradition began to dwindle somewhat in the late 19th century.
In 1860 the journalist İbrahim Şinasi (1826–1871) wrote what is noted as the first modern Turkish play. It was a one-act comedy called Şair Evlenmesi, meaning The Poet's Marriage.
The poet Namık Kemal (1840–1888) also wrote the important 1876 novel İntibâh, meaning Awakening. It shows how a Tanzimat writer moved between poetry and the newly arrived form of the novel.

Ahmed Midhat Efendi (1844–1912) wrote important novels in three major movements. These were Romanticism with Hasan Mellâh in 1873, Realism with Henüz On Yedi Yaşında in 1881, and Naturalism with Müşâhedât in 1891.

The magazine Genç Kalemler, meaning Young Pens, was begun in the city of Selânik in 1911. Its founders were the sociologist Ziya Gökalp, the short-story writer Ömer Seyfettin and the poet Ali Canip Yöntem, and it became the center of the National Literature movement.

Ottoman poets openly wrote about same-sex love and desire until the 19th century. The homoerotic poems were long believed to be exclusively pederastic, with older men desiring boys. That was the norm, but some poems described relationships between post-pubescent males of similar ages, or younger males taking the insertive role in anal intercourse. Hamse pentalogies also featured erotic miniature paintings of sexual scenes. Then Westernization led to the stigmatization of homosexuality, and it is possible that some literary scenes of a homosexual nature were later removed by censors, once heterosexuality had become more normative.
literature.source_title: Sexual and gender minorities in the Ottoman Empire

literature.text: Ottoman Turkish was written in the Perso-Arabic script. During the rise of Turkish nationalism in the nineteenth century, Turkish intellectuals sought to simplify the written language.

Genç Kalemler's first issue carried an article titled New Language, or Yeni Lisan. It pointed out that Turkish literature had looked either East, to the Ottoman Divan tradition, or West, to the Edebiyyât-ı Cedîde and Fecr-i Âtî movements, without ever turning to Turkey itself.

Much Ottoman prose was expected to follow the rules of sec', or rhymed prose, which prescribed that a rhyme must fall between each adjective and noun in a sentence. This is a large part of why prose never developed as far as Divan poetry before the 19th century.
Towards the end of the 19th century, popular literature such as newspapers began to be published in the Azerbaijani language. Before that, its written literature had been dominated by poetry.

The aşıks, whose tradition declined in the 19th century, were minstrels who travelled through Anatolia performing on the bağlama. This mandolin-like instrument has paired strings that are considered to have a symbolic religious significance in Alevi/Bektashi culture.

science.text: Railway stations became a feature of Ottoman modernisation, reflecting the new infrastructure changes within the empire. The most famous example is the Sirkeci Railway Station, built in 1888 to 1890 as the terminus of the Orient Express.

The Tersâne-i Âmire, the imperial shipyard on the Golden Horn, had fallen into neglect and underinvestment by the reign of Abdulmejid I (1839 to 1861). He started a massive investment programme that modernised it, and also the shipyards in Izmit and Gemlik.
science.source_title: Army of the classical Ottoman Empire

science.text: In 1827 Sultan Mahmud II founded the Ottoman Empire's first medical school, modeled on those in the West. Teaching was at first in French, and most instructors and students were non-Muslims, including Armenians, Arab Christians, Bulgarians and Greeks.

The world's first successful oil tanker was Zoroaster, designed for Ludvig Nobel with Sven Alexander Almqvist. By putting the oil in tanks, they solved the problem of a bulk liquid cargo making a ship unstable. It made its first run from Baku to Astrakhan in 1878.

Pipeline transport was pioneered near Baku by Vladimir Shukhov and the Branobel company between 1878 and 1880. Branobel itself began as a distillery founded by Robert and Ludvig Nobel in Baku in 1876.

Dmitri Mendeleev proposed a Baku to Batum pipeline in 1880 to carry Baku oil to the world market. Vladimir Shukhov later designed the technical project. When the first section, Batum to Mikhailovo (Khashuri), was finished in 1906, it was the world's longest kerosene pipeline.

The Tiflis Botanical Garden was revived in the early 19th century after being pillaged in the Persian invasion of 1795. It was officially established in 1845, and a floristics center was set up there in 1888.

The Anatolian Railway's first line ran from Haydarpaşa to Pendik and opened on 22 September 1872, built under Sultan Abdulaziz. It reached İzmit in August 1873. In 1892 the company ran the first passenger train between Istanbul and Ankara, a daily service.

Ludvig Nobel refused to patent any part of the Zoroaster's design, so it was widely studied and copied. In October 1878 he ordered two more tankers of the same design, the Buddha and the Nordenskjöld.
Between 1877 and 1901, Branobel drilled over 500 wells, produced 150 million barrels of oil and employed 12,000 workers. By 1916 it was the largest oil company in Russia.

In 1873 Robert Nobel was sent to the Caucasus to buy walnut wood for rifle stocks. Without consulting his brother, he spent the 25,000 rubles, called the walnut money, on a small refinery in Baku instead. By 1876 the Nobel brothers had established themselves as the most competent refiner in Baku and Batumi.

Funded by the Russian-Armenian oil tycoon Alexander Mantashev, the Baku–Batumi pipeline was officially opened in Tiflis on 24 July 1907. Its construction had been delayed for years: in 1891 it was postponed as premature, and the government decision to proceed came only in 1893.

In 1897 the Anatolian Railway built a new port at Derince near İzmit, because Haydarpaşa's equipment could not cope with the traffic. The Derince port had a grain elevator to export grain from central Anatolia.

politics.text: On 15 June 1826, Sultan Mahmud II forced the old Ottoman standing army to disband in what is known as the Auspicious Incident. It followed a century-long reform effort, and the Humbaracı Ocağı, the bombardier corps, supported the government that day.
politics.source_title: Army of the classical Ottoman Empire

politics.text: In 1844 the Ottoman Empire officially adopted a national flag: a red field with a white five-pointed star and crescent. The choice was part of the Tanzimat reforms, which aimed to bring the Ottoman state in line with the laws and norms of contemporary European states.

Abdul Hamid II was the 34th Sultan, ruling from 31 August 1876 until he was deposed on 27 April 1909. He oversaw a period of decline in the power and extent of the empire, and was the last Ottoman Sultan to rule with absolute power.

Up to 1850, the Ottoman Empire was the only empire to have never contracted foreign debt. The Crimean War of 1853–1856 made such debt necessary. The first foreign loan came in 1854, when western powers began sporadic attempts to impose some control.
politics.source_title: Economic history of the Ottoman Empire

politics.text: Russia made an alliance with the eastern Georgian kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti in 1783, under Heraclius II, making it a Russian protectorate. But Russia was unwilling to fulfill the treaty's terms and annexed the kingdom in 1801, reducing it to the Georgia Governorate. Russian General Knorring had secret orders to remove all the male and some female members of the royal family to Russia, and in April 1802 he held the nobility in Tbilisi's Sioni Cathedral and forced them to take an oath on the imperial crown of Russia; those who disagreed were arrested. In 1810 the western kingdom of Imereti was annexed as well, after a Russian decree dethroned Solomon II and a large Russian army invaded; many Imeretians fled to the forests to resist, and the Russians crushed the guerrilla uprising.

In 1875, with external debt at 242 million Turkish pounds and over half of budget spending going to service it, the Ottoman government declared it could not make repayments. The Public Debt Administration was then set up, subjecting the Ottomans to foreign financial control. In 1914 the debt still stood at 139.1 million Turkish pounds.
politics.source_title: Economic history of the Ottoman Empire

politics.text: Beginning in 1839, the Ottoman government implemented the Tanzimat reforms, aiming among other goals to improve the situation of non-Muslim minorities. In 1856 the Imperial Reform Edict promised equality for all Ottoman citizens irrespective of ethnicity and confession, widening the scope of the 1839 Edict of Gülhane, though the reforms proved largely ineffective.

A Constitution written by members of the Young Ottomans was promulgated on 23 November 1876. It established freedom of belief and equality of all citizens before the law, and it marked the peak of the reformist period.

For most of Ottoman history the sultan was the absolute monarch, head of state and head of government. During the First Constitutional Era (1876–1878) and the Second (1908–1920), the empire shifted to a constitutional monarchy, with the Grand Vizier taking a prime ministerial role and heading an elected General Assembly.

From 1894 to 1896, between 80,000 and 300,000 Armenians living throughout the empire were killed in what became known as the Hamidian massacres. The massacres are named for Sultan Abdul Hamid II, whose efforts to reinforce the empire's territorial integrity resulted in them.

By 1875 the Ottoman external debt stood at 242 million Turkish pounds, and over half the budget went to servicing it. Bad harvests and the costs of suppressing the uprisings in the Balkans hastened the slide into bankruptcy. The government declared it could not make repayments.
politics.source_title: Economic history of the Ottoman Empire

politics.text: In 1844, a red flag with a white five-pointed star and crescent was officially adopted as the Ottoman national flag. The decision was part of the Tanzimat reforms, which aimed to modernize the Ottoman state along the lines of contemporary European states.

Qajar Iran lost much of its Caucasian territory to Russia in the first decades of the 19th century, including modern-day eastern Georgia, Dagestan, Azerbaijan and Armenia. The losses were formalised by the treaties of Gulistan in 1813 and Turkmenchay in 1828, after two Russo-Persian wars.

As part of the Tanzimat reforms, the Anatolia Eyalet, one of the two core provinces of the early Ottoman Empire, was dissolved c. 1841 and divided into smaller provinces. Scholars give conflicting dates for this, from as early as 1832 to as late as 1864.

In 1896, Dashnaks armed with pistols, grenades, dynamite and hand-held bombs seized the Ottoman Bank in Constantinople for 14 hours, and 10 of the Armenian men and Ottoman soldiers died. The Porte's reaction brought further massacres and pogroms of the several thousand Armenians living in Constantinople, and Sultan Abdul Hamid II threatened to level the entire building. European diplomats persuaded the government to give the survivors safe passage to France.

Austria-Hungary officially annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1908, profiting from civil strife in the empire. The Ottomans then lost their North African territories and the Dodecanese in the Italo-Turkish War (1911), and almost all their European territories in the Balkan Wars (1912–1913). Two further coups came in 1912 and 1913.

After negotiations with the European powers, the Public Debt Administration was set up and certain Ottoman revenues were assigned to it. This subjected the Ottomans to foreign financial control that they failed to escape. In 1914 the debt stood at 139.1 million Turkish pounds.
politics.source_title: Economic history of the Ottoman Empire

politics.text: In 1804 Pavel Tsitsianov, commander of Russian forces in the Caucasus, attacked Ganja, provoking the Russo-Persian War of 1804 to 1813. Georgians were divided: some fought as volunteers helping the Russian army, while others rebelled, and there was a major uprising in the highlands of Kartli-Kakheti in 1804. It ended in Russian victory, with Persia recognising the tsar's claims over Georgia in the Treaty of Gulistan.

Mingrelia was a Russian protectorate from 1803 but was not absorbed until 1867. The Principality of Guria was abolished in 1829, and Svaneti was gradually annexed in 1858. Georgia was taken in piece by piece over the century.

philosophy.text: The Ottoman term millet came into systematic use for non-Muslim communities under Sultan Mahmud II (r. 1808-1839). Official documents of his time stated that non-Muslim subjects were organized into three sanctioned millets: Greek Orthodox, Armenian, and Jewish.

During the 19th century rise of nationalism, the Tanzimat reforms (1839-76) led to the word millet being used for legally protected ethno-linguistic minority groups. Yet the Ottoman state defined each millet by religion rather than ethnicity, and Muslims were not counted as a millet.

Miletus, on the western coast of Anatolia, was the home of the Milesian school of thinkers Thales, Anaximander, and Anaximenes. Its first excavations were led by French archaeologist Olivier Rayet in 1873. German archaeologists Julius Hülsen and Theodor Wiegand then worked there between 1899 and 1931.

Nineteenth-century Ottoman bureaucrats claimed the millet system dated back to Sultan Mehmed I (r. 1413-1421). Recent scholarship shows it was actually a later political innovation, introduced in the rhetorical garb of an ancient tradition.

The Syriac Catholic community was recognized as its own millet in 1829, and the Chaldean Catholic community in 1844. The Syriac Orthodox had long been counted under the Armenian Patriarch, and only won their own millet in 1873 during the Tanzimat reforms.

One remarkable find from the first 19th-century excavations at Miletus, the Market Gate, was transported piece by piece to Germany and reassembled. It is now exhibited at the Pergamon Museum in Berlin, while the main collection stays in the Miletus Museum in Didim.

culture.text: In 1844, the Ottoman Empire officially adopted a red flag with a white five-pointed star and crescent as its national flag. The decision was part of the Tanzimat reforms, which aimed to modernize the state in line with contemporary European states and institutions.

Football became popular in 19th-century Constantinople, and European-model sports clubs followed. Beşiktaş Gymnastics Club was founded in 1903, Galatasaray Sports Club in 1905 and Fenerbahçe Sports Club in 1907.

Clock towers rose to prominence in the Ottoman Empire over the 19th century. Mahmud II erected the oldest clock tower in Istanbul, the Tophane Clock Tower, between 1835 and 1839, and Abdülmecid rebuilt it in more monumental form in 1848 or 1849.

Parisian-style shopping arcades appeared in the Beyoğlu district of Istanbul in the 19th century. The best-known example is the Çiçek Pasajı, or Flower Passage, built in 1876 as part of the Cité de Pera, with shops on the ground floor and luxury apartments above.

The main sports Ottomans engaged in were Turkish wrestling, hunting, Turkish archery, horseback riding, equestrian javelin throw, arm wrestling and swimming. Football and European-style clubs arrived alongside these older pursuits in the 19th century.

Under Sultan Mahmud II, official documents in the early 19th century began systematically using the word millet for non-Muslim communities. They were organized into three officially sanctioned millets: Greek Orthodox, Armenian and Jewish. Recent scholarship suggests this was a later political innovation presented as an ancient tradition.
Footballs clubs also formed outside the capital. In İzmir, Karşıyaka Sports Club was founded in 1912, and Altay Sports Club and Turkish Fatherland Football Club, later Ülküspor, followed in 1914.

In 1870, the Ottoman sultan Abdulaziz officially set up the Bulgarian Orthodox Exarchate. The Patriarchate of Constantinople declared it schismatic and an ethno-nationalist heresy, ending a decades-long Bulgarian struggle over church autonomy.

The Hazzopulo Pasajı in Beyoğlu was a shopping arcade with a small courtyard filled with shops and surrounded by buildings. It was begun in 1850 and completed in 1871, and it shows how long such Parisian-style projects could take.

The Syriac Orthodox were long treated as part of the Armenian millet under the Armenian Patriarch, which left them subject to Armenian hegemony linguistically, culturally, politically and religiously. During the Tanzimat reforms they were granted independent status, with their own millet recognized in 1873.
